svg.text: HER POV / VOL. 02
THE REPLY DECODER
A DIFFERENT WAY TO CONNECT
CHAPTER 02
The S.I.G.N.A.L. Check
Six questions that replace overanalysis
S — Substance: is there something specific to respond to? I — Invitation: did they ask a question, add a topic,
or suggest a next step? G — Give-and-take: is effort mutual over time? N — Natural pace: does your reply fit
the actual rhythm rather than a strategy invented online? A — Autonomy: is the other person free to stop,
slow down, or say no without pressure? L — Long view: what does the recent pattern suggest, and how little
can you safely conclude?
This is a reflection tool, not a scoring system. A reply that lacks a question may still be friendly. A long answer
may still be polite rather than romantic. Use the questions to decide what
you
want to do next, not to label a
stranger with certainty.
Situation one: short but specific
You write: "Have you found a decent hiking trail around here?" She replies: "Eagle Creek is my favorite."
Substance: yes. Invitation: not explicit. Give-and-take: not known. A reasonable reply: "Nice, I've heard of that
one. Is it a tougher hike or more of a relaxed afternoon?" If she remains engaged, continue. If not, there's no
need to force it.
Situation two: enthusiastic but unavailable
She writes: "I would love to hear the story! I'm traveling and probably won't be on here much." Substance and
warmth are present; availability is limited. Don't punish the delay or demand check-ins. "Have an amazing trip.
We can pick this up whenever you're back" preserves interest and autonomy.
Situation three: the clear boundary
She writes: "I'm not interested in meeting." There is nothing to decode. Treat the words as decisive.
"Understood. Wishing you the best" is enough if a response is appropriate; silence is also acceptable. Never
counterargue, guilt, or try to earn another chance.
